newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica white maize firm but Kenya buying to slow.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica white maize firm but Kenya buying to slow.

text.p: Forward-dated South African white maize futures have started rising, lifted by concerns of a possible shortage this year due to large-scale exports and worries that the El Nino weather phenomenon may hit in December.

However, market sources said on Monday that some of the price pressure would be relieved as exports to Kenya -- the biggest export destination this year -- dried up in September when that country's harvest kicked in and it brought back suspended duties and taxes on maize imports.

"It is very unlikely that imports will continue (after August) as our harvest starts in late August and September...And such a huge quantity has already been brought in," said a spokesman for Kenya's Famine Early Warning System (FEWS).

The spokesman for the project, which falls under the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), said that around 350,000 tonnes of white maize had been imported during July and August, mostly from South Africa. This was well above an expected 180,000 tonnes.
Imports follow a prolonged drought in Kenya which prompted the government in January to remove duties and taxes on imported maize for relief feeding and strategic reserves.
The temporary scrapping of duties, which was extended for a two-month period in June, was unlikely to be renewed, the FEWS spokesman said.
White maize contracts on South Africa's Futures Exchange on Monday added nine rand to 635.00 rand and the further-dated December contract rose five to 670.00.

Traders said that the rise came on the back of comments by the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) on Friday that there would be a 476,000 tonne shortage of white maize this season. Price rises were also fuelled by market concerns about the possibility of an El Nino-inspired drought next season.

"If you take a look at how much Durban can export, Nampo may not be exaggerating the shortage. The probability is that 1.3 million tonnes can go out...And with a possible El Nino, do you want to take the chance that there will not be any white maize?" one trader said.

Global weather analysts have expressed concerns over the early build-up and intensity of El Nino, which has the potential to cause devastating droughts on one side of the globe while spurring floods elsewhere.

The country's monthly crop estimate was last week raised to 7.966 million tonnes from 7.660 million in June. The crop was expected to comprise 4.333 million tonnes of white and 3.633 million of yellow.
Yellow maize futures contracts have continued to trend lower as some white maize, damaged by late rains and extreme cold, competes with yellow in the animal feed market, sources said.
September yellow was last bid at 530.00 rand from a 535 rand settlement and December at 566.00 from 575.
